claims.text: Removing specific alloying elements alters local chemical disorder in equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni subsets.
Changes in local chemical disorder alter stacking fault energy.
Stacking fault energy modulates dislocation dissociation and deformation-twin formation.
The quinary, quaternary, and ternary alloys have single-phase FCC microstructures after the specified thermomechanical processing.
Identical uniaxial tensile tests provide the controlled comparison among the quinary, quaternary, and ternary alloys.
Fixing temperature and strain rate while matching grain size and thermomechanical history is intended to prevent processing variation from confounding the comparison.
The full five-element composition produces greater local chemical disorder than the quaternary and ternary subsets.
The quinary alloy has an SFE that favors a balance between dislocation glide and deformation-twin formation.
Reducing the number of constituent elements modifies the local chemical environment and changes SFE.
The altered SFE in the subsets changes dislocation behavior and twin nucleation.
Changes in dislocation behavior and twin nucleation affect work hardening and failure mode.
Relative to the quinary baseline, the quaternary and ternary alloys are expected to have lower work-hardening rates.
Relative to the quinary baseline, the quaternary and ternary alloys are expected to have altered ductility.
The predicted differences in work hardening and ductility result from suppressed or otherwise modified twin formation.
The hypothesis is limited to similarly processed, single-phase FCC microstructures tested near room temperature at controlled strain rate and comparable microstructural state.
A lack of significant SFE and twin-formation differences relative to the quinary baseline would falsify the hypothesis.
A lack of correlation between mechanical-property changes and the measured SFE or twin-formation changes would falsify the hypothesis.
